ta-l1d15q4-d1e3498.summary: A divisio textus for the part of Distinction 15 on the special modes of the Son's mission. Lombard asks whether the Son was sent once or is sent often and distinguishes two modes, the visible mission in the flesh and the invisible mission into minds, assigning two differences between them. He then answers why the Father is not said to be sent although he is known by someone in time: because authority of principle is in him. He refutes heretics who inferred from this that the Father is greater and the Son lesser. Thomas announces inquiries into the Son's invisible mission in itself (the visible mission being left for Book III) and in relation to those to whom it is made. The first has three articles: whether invisible mission belongs to the Son, whether it is distinct from the Spirit's invisible mission, and whether any mission is eternal.
claims: The Son is sent visibly in the flesh and invisibly into minds.
The Father is not sent because authority of principle is in him, which does not make him greater.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3534.summary: First objection that the Son is not sent invisibly into the mind. Mission requires that the arriving person be known, especially in the mission of wisdom, which no one who has it is ignorant of. But the Son's coming is not known: 'if he comes to me, I shall not understand' (Job 9:11).
claims: Mission requires knowledge of the arriving person.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3540.summary: Second objection. Mission is temporal procession, and procession is called temporal only by its relation to that into which it is, which the Spirit's procession has from its mode as love. The Son's procession by its mode has no relation 'into which', only 'from which', so temporal procession and mission do not fit the Son.
claims: The Son's procession has no relation to an object, unlike love's.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3543.summary: Third objection. A divine person is sent only in sanctifying gifts, but the intellectual gifts appropriated to the Son are not sanctifying, being common to good and bad ('if I have all knowledge but have not charity, I am nothing', 1 Cor. 13).
claims: Intellectual gifts are common to the good and the wicked.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3550.summary: Sed contra from Wisdom 9:10, 'send her (wisdom) from your heavens'. This is not essential wisdom, which is not from another and so not sent, but begotten wisdom, the Son.
claims: Begotten wisdom, the Son, is sent.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3562.summary: Second sed contra from Augustine: as the Son's being begotten is his being from the Father, his being sent is his being known to be from the Father, which happens.
claims: The Son's mission is his being known as from the Father.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3568.summary: Thomas's determination. As in the going out of things from the principle divine goodness is said to proceed into creatures by being represented in them through a received likeness, so in the bringing back of the rational creature to God a divine person proceeds, which is called mission. The person's proper relation is represented in the soul by a received likeness modelled on and originating from that eternal relational property. The Spirit's proper mode of relating to the Father is love, and the Son's is being the Word who manifests him. So as the Spirit proceeds invisibly into the mind by the gift of love, the Son proceeds by the gift of wisdom, in which the Father, the last end to which we return, is manifested. Since by receiving these gifts a likeness to the persons' properties is produced in us, the persons are said to be in us in a new mode of being, as a thing is in its likeness, and both processions are called missions. Moreover, as these gifts originate from the persons' properties, they achieve their effect of joining us to the end only by the persons' power, since the power of the one impressing is in the impressed form. So in receiving these gifts the persons are had in a new way as leaders to the end or as uniting us to it, and both processions are called giving.
claims: The Son is sent invisibly by the gift of wisdom, as the Spirit by the gift of love.
Mission consists in a received likeness of the person's proper relation, in which the person is newly present.
The persons are had in a new way through these gifts, as uniting us to the end.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3571.summary: Reply to the first objection. Mission requires not actual but habitual knowledge of the person, insofar as the gift conferred, a habit, represents the person's property as a likeness. That is how 'to be sent is to be known to be from another' is meant, by way of representation, as something manifests itself by representing itself in its likeness. Still, I cannot know with certainty that I have the gift in which a divine person is given, because moral acts resemble meritorious ones, though I can conjecture from signs, unless certainty comes by revelation. Hence Job's words: sanctifying grace, in which the person comes, cannot be known with certainty, though the gift itself is sufficient to lead to knowledge of the person who comes.
claims: Mission requires habitual, representational knowledge of the person, not actual knowledge.
One cannot know with certainty that one has sanctifying grace, except by revelation.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3577.summary: Reply to the second objection. The Spirit's property, love, can relate to the creature in two ways: as object, or as exemplar principle to what is exemplified. The Son's property can have only the second relation, as principle, and this suffices for the Son's temporal procession, though the Spirit's temporal procession involves more relations. So mission can belong to both.
claims: The Son's temporal procession rests on his property as exemplar principle of the gift.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3580.summary: Reply to the third objection. When something is participated not in its perfect act but in some way, it is not properly said to be had, as animals have something of prudence but not prudence, lacking the act of reason that is choice. There are two grades of knowledge: the intellect's tending to the one, and its taking the true as fitting and good. Unless something resists, love and delight follow, since delight follows perfect, unimpeded operation, and contemplative happiness is reaching and exercising the intellect's ultimate operation without hindrance. In the procession of the eternal Word there is knowledge perfect in every way, so love proceeds from it, as Augustine says the Word is knowledge with love. So whenever there is knowledge from which gratuitous love does not follow, there is not a likeness of the Word, only something of it. There is a likeness of the Word only when there is knowledge from which proceeds love that joins one to what is known as fitting. Only one who receives such knowledge has the Son dwelling in them, and this cannot be without sanctifying grace. So, simply and properly, the Son is given and sent only in the gift of sanctifying grace, while other gifts of knowledge share something of the Word's likeness.
claims: The Word is knowledge breathing forth love; only knowledge from which love proceeds is a likeness of the Word.
The Son is sent properly only in sanctifying grace; other gifts of knowledge share only something of his likeness.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3595.summary: First argument that the Son's mission is distinct from the Spirit's. Mission is temporal procession, and the Son's and the Spirit's processions differ in character, as Word and as love.
claims: Son and Spirit proceed differently, as Word and as love.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3598.summary: Second argument. What belongs to things by priority and posteriority does not belong to them in the same sense. Giving belongs to the Spirit before the Son, since he has the character of first gift, so giving and mission differ in the two.
claims: Giving belongs first to the Spirit as first gift.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3601.summary: Third argument. The gifts in which Son and Spirit are given are diverse and independent, and of independent things one can exist without the other, so the missions can be separated even in time.
claims: Independent gifts can occur without each other.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3605.summary: Fourth argument. We see simple people fervent in divine love who are dull in knowledge of divine wisdom, and conversely. So one mission can exist without the other.
claims: Fervent love can coexist with little knowledge.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3608.summary: Sed contra. The Spirit's mission is for sanctifying the creature. If the Son's mission, also in sanctifying grace, were another mission, there would be two missions for sanctifying, and one would be superfluous, which is not found in God's works.
claims: Two missions for sanctification would be superfluous.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3611.summary: Thomas's determination. The distinction of the missions can be discussed as to their real diversity, as to the concept of mission, or as to their separability. (1) Really, both elements of mission differ: the Son's going out by generation differs from the Spirit's by procession, and the gift perfecting the intellect, wisdom, differs from the gift perfecting affection or will. (2) As to concept, by the common concept the missions are the same in both elements, since being from another and being newly in the creature are common to both; by the proper concept they differ, since the Son proceeds as Son or Word and the Spirit as love, and the Son is in the creature by wisdom, the Spirit by love. (3) As to separation, one mission is never without the other: love follows knowledge, and the perfect knowledge by which the Son is sent always leads into love, so they are infused together and increase together.
claims: The missions of Son and Spirit differ really and by proper concept but share a common concept.
The two missions are never separated: the perfect knowledge of the Son's mission always leads into the love of the Spirit's.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3614.summary: Reply to the first argument. Though the processions differ really, they share a common concept, being from another.
claims: The processions share the common concept of being from another.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3617.summary: Reply to the second argument. There is no prior and posterior in God, but the Spirit's going out presupposes the Son's by order of nature, so in respect of going out the Son's mission could, so to speak, be called prior, by the proper and not the common concept. As to the effect in the creature, one can consider the gifts or the giver. On the side of the gifts, knowledge naturally precedes love, so the Son's mission precedes the Spirit's, again by the proper concept, as all species of motion share equally in the common concept while local motion is prior in its own being. On the side of the giver, since the first mover inclining to give is love, the giving of the Spirit is prior to that of the Son, though this is not expressed in the concept of mission.
claims: By order of nature and of gifts the Son's mission is prior; on the side of the giver, the Spirit's giving is prior, since love moves to give.
concepts: love as first motive of giving

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3620.summary: Reply to the third argument. The gifts in which Son and Spirit are sent necessarily follow each other, so the argument proceeds from a false premise.
claims: The gifts of wisdom and love necessarily accompany each other.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3624.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The knowledge from which love proceeds flourishes in those fervent in divine love: they know divine goodness as end and as pouring its benefits most abundantly on them. Those not set on fire with love of God do not perfectly have such knowledge.
claims: The knowledge relevant to the Son's mission is affective knowledge of God's goodness, found in the fervent.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3627.summary: Reply to the sed contra. Both missions are ordered to one last end, joining us to God, but their effects differ according to the two things in the rational creature by which it is joined to God, intellect and affection, so neither is superfluous.
claims: The two missions perfect intellect and affection respectively and so are not superfluous.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3639.summary: First argument that mission can be eternal. Gregory says the Son is sent by that by which he is begotten, and his generation is eternal.
claims: Gregory: the Son is sent by that by which he is begotten.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3642.summary: Second argument. Like mission, the procession of love implies a relation 'from which' and 'into which', and the procession of love is eternal, from the Father into the Son.
claims: Love proceeds eternally from the Father into the Son.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3645.summary: Third argument. 'Gift', like mission, is said by relation to the creature, and the Spirit is called gift from eternity.
claims: The Spirit is gift from eternity.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3649.summary: Sed contra from Augustine in Lombard's text: the Son is not said to be sent by the fact that he is born of the Father.
claims: The Son's birth is not his mission.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3655.summary: Second sed contra, adopted as the answer. Mission always implies a new mode of existing in something of the one sent, and nothing new is eternal. So mission is not eternal but only temporal, which is to be granted simply.
claims: Mission implies newness and so is only temporal.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3658.summary: Reply to the first argument. Gregory's statement can be read in three ways: as concerning the Son's temporal generation, by which he is sent in the flesh; with 'eo' as an ablative, 'he is sent by him by whom he is begotten', which is true; or as concerning mission not in act but in aptitude, since by going out from the Father by generation the Son is, so to speak, 'sendable'. Being from another is not the whole concept of mission.
claims: Gregory's dictum can be read of temporal generation, of the sender's identity, or of aptitude for mission.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3661.summary: Reply to the second argument. The procession of love, though into someone, does not imply a new mode of existing in them and so can be eternal. Mission implies newness of existing in someone and so cannot be eternal. So although it can in some way be granted that the Spirit proceeds from the Father into the Son from eternity, it is not granted that he is sent from the Father into the Son from eternity.
claims: The Spirit proceeds eternally into the Son but is not sent into the Son.

ta-l1d15q4-d1e3664.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Mission' is a verbal noun and implies an actual relation to the creature, but 'gift' is imposed from aptitude for giving and implies no actual relation, so the Spirit is called gift from eternity but not sent or given from eternity.
claims: 'Gift' names aptitude and so is eternal; 'mission' names an actual relation and so is temporal.

ta-l1d15q4-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Question 4 maps Lombard's distinction between the Son's visible and invisible missions and his explanation that the Father is not sent because he has authority of principle, without being greater. It announces three articles on the Son's invisible mission.

ta-l1d15q4-Dd1e3526.summary: Article 1 asks whether the Son is sent invisibly into the mind. Thomas holds that as divine goodness proceeds into creatures by likeness in their going out, so in their return a divine person proceeds by a received likeness of its proper relation. The Spirit is sent by the gift of love and the Son by the gift of wisdom, which manifests the Father. Mission requires only habitual, representational knowledge, and the possession of grace cannot be known with certainty without revelation. The Son is sent properly only in sanctifying grace, because only knowledge from which love proceeds is a likeness of the Word, who breathes forth love.
claims: The Son is sent invisibly by the gift of wisdom from which love proceeds.
Mission involves habitual knowledge; possession of grace is not certainly knowable.

ta-l1d15q4-Dd1e3587.summary: Article 2 asks whether the Son's invisible mission is distinct from the Spirit's. The missions differ really and by proper concept: the Son proceeds by generation and through wisdom, perfecting the intellect, and the Spirit by procession and through love, perfecting affection. They share a common concept, being from another and newly present. They are never separated, since perfect knowledge always leads into love. The Son's mission is prior by order of nature and of gifts, the Spirit's on the side of the giver, since love moves to give.
claims: The two missions differ really but are inseparable.
They perfect intellect and affection, both ordered to union with God.

ta-l1d15q4-Dd1e3631.summary: Article 3 asks whether any mission is eternal. Thomas holds that mission is only temporal, because it implies a new mode of existing in the recipient. Gregory's dictum refers to temporal generation, to the identity of the sender, or to aptitude. The Spirit proceeds eternally into the Son but is not sent into him, and 'gift' names an eternal aptitude while 'mission' names an actual, temporal relation.
claims: Mission is only temporal; the Spirit is eternally gift but not eternally sent.

ta-l1d15q4.summary: Quaestio 4 of Book I, Distinction 15 treats the Son's invisible mission. Article 1 holds that as divine goodness proceeds into creatures by likeness in their going out, so in the return of the rational creature the persons proceed by received likenesses of their proper relations: the Spirit by love, the Son by wisdom. The Son is properly sent only in sanctifying grace, since only knowledge breathing forth love is a likeness of the Word, and one cannot know with certainty that one has it. Article 2 holds that the two missions differ really and in proper concept, perfecting intellect and affection, but are inseparable and share a common concept. Article 3 holds that mission is only temporal, since it implies newness, while 'gift' can be eternal.
claims: The Son is sent invisibly by the gift of a wisdom from which love proceeds.
The missions of Son and Spirit are distinct but inseparable, perfecting intellect and affection.
Mission is only temporal.
